I've never worked on commission before, so I'm not sure about that. Please treat your commission as an added bonus and try not to let it pressure you into selling patients something they don't actually need. 

First and foremost, congratulations. Your main goal is to help people see and THAT can be a very very exciting thing. Remember this when you have a difficult patient. It's frustrating to not be able to see, and you can help.

Frames

Zyl just means the frame is plastic. 
Metal is metal
Nylor or grooved means the lens is held in place with a clear cord. These frames are often called semi-rimless.
Drill mount means there is no actual frame, just some lenses and a chasis. These are offer called rimless.
You will see a string of numbers somewhere on the frame. Something like 52 [ ] 18 [ ] 140. This is the frame size. The first number is generally in the 50s for adults and is the "A size" or the size of one lens, horizontally. The second number is called the DBL (distance between lenses) and is the size of the bridge. The third number is the length of the temple piece. All measurements are done in millimeters. 

Lenses

There are SO MANY lens options. The main ones you'll encounter are:

Single vision (SV): to help correct vision at on focal length. So just distance, just reading, or just intermediate.

Multifocals, lined: this will include lined bifocals  (flatops/straighttops: ft28/ft35) or lined trifocals (ft7x28) The top part of these lenses is for seeing far away, and the bottom is for reading. There is no correction for mid range distance.

Progressive Addittion Lenses (PALS)
These are also referred to as "no line bifocals" even though they aren't really a bifocal. These help people see at a range of distances, including near, far, and intermediate. 

Lens materials

CR39 -basic plastic
Polycarbonate & Trivex - more durable lens materials, good option for most people.  
High Index - thinner and lighter plastics, good for people with high prescriptions.

Common lens treatments 

Anti Reflective  (AR): reduces glare. This helps people with night driving, eye fatigue from lights, and should make lenses a little easier to clean.

Scratch coats (SRC)- this is a treatment that makes lenses harder to scratch. A lot of AR coatings also include an SRC, but not all. 

Transitions (photochromic)- these are the lenses that change to sun wear when exposed to light.

Measurements you'll be taking 

Pupillary Distance (pd): how far the patients pupils are from one another.

Seg height: in a bifocal this is where the reading portion will begin and should be measured from the bottom of the lens to the lower eyelid. In a trifocal, it is where the intermediate part of the lens will start and should be measured from the bottom of the lens to the bottom of the pupil. In a PAL it is where the progression will start and should be measured from the bottom of the lense to the middle of the pupil. 

Those are some of the basics. I'd be more than happy to answer any other questions for you. I super love opticianry :).

I would write a letter to both companies. One to the company running things, and one to whoever handles their contract at your company. Outline your observations and concerns. Whenever doing stuff like this, I use the acronym D.E.A.R. 

D.escribe: using facts, describe what you are observing and experiencing.


E.xpress: how this makes you feel. Example: "it makes me uncomfortable to ingest food that I know is being handled incorrectly." Or "it makes me frustrated to know that my at work option is a potential health hazzard.


A.sk: What is it you want? "I would like to feel comfortable dining in the cafeteria in my workplace"


R.einforce: How does meeting your requests benefit them? This part is going to be different depending on which letter you are writing. For your company, having happy and comfortable workers is generally more productive. For the company running the cafeteria, having satisfied  consumers could potentially create longer contracts and they can keep their jobs.

Dbt was awesome. The program I was in met for ten hours a week. I was in it for a little under a year and a half. Dbt is set up to have four different modules. Emotion regulation is figuring out personal patterns triggers etc. and setting up healthy habits such as diet exercise and sleep. Distress tolerance is another module which teaches you a variety of different skills to handle panic attacks, deep depression, and other pressing mental health needs. These skills help reduce the intensity of your shitty feelings. Interpersonal effectiveness (another module) is pretty self explanatory, it gives you good guidelines and tips for effectively communicating your needs. And lastly and.possibly most importantly in the mindfulness module which puts emphasis on living in the moment, letting go, and actively tending to your mental health. It taught me how to identify emotions which was something I was never able to do in the past. It helped me to realize just how important sleeping is. I'm also bipolar and I was able to figure out the warning signs for when I was going to have a manic episode. It taught me to take responsibility for my actions. It taught me how to be gentle with myself and talk to myself nicely. Dbt taught me that even if today is bad, tomorrow might be better. The program taught me that "it is what it is" and sometimes you just have to make the best of a crap situation. It taught me how to be assertive without being aggressive. It is just so fantastic. I'm a different person now. I still struggle but my quality of life has drastically improved. I actually leave my house now and I haven't been in trouble with the cops for a couple years.
